input.prompt: First-person view of a plague doctor standing in a cramped one-room home of a poor family in a remote mountain village, present day, late afternoon: plain painted walls with a few damp stains and nothing hanging on them except a small wooden crucifix; on the left an old black cast-iron wood stove, cold, with its small front door ajar and a folded white cloth stuffed inside instead of firewood; next to it a tiny kitchen corner with a chipped enamel sink and a two-burner gas cooker; on the right an unmade double bed with an iron headboard, a thin mattress and a crumpled brown blanket, and next to the bed a worn brown armchair with a small table beside it holding an old nebulizer machine; at the back a window with half-closed plastic roller blinds. A ceiling lamp gives even light. Two people face the viewer in tense silence. In the middle of the room stands a tired, hard-faced woman in her fifties with her arms crossed, in a shapeless dark grey cardigan over a faded housedress and worn slippers, her greying hair tied back carelessly: she has just woken up after a night shift. On the right, in the worn armchair next to the bed, sits her husband in his sixties, a heavy-boned, wasted former quarry worker with grey stubble and a shaved head, in an old vest under a brown wool blanket wrapped around his shoulders and legs, the plastic mask of the nebulizer hanging on his chest, struggling to breathe. They are hiding something, and their faces show it. No hands, arms or objects belonging to the viewer are visible in the frame. Realistic photograph, evenly exposed, everything clearly readable, no dramatic shadows. 16:9, no text, no border.

Completely re-render this image in the style described below, transforming it far beyond a filter: redraw every surface, light and texture in that technique. Keep the composition: the cold wood stove with its door ajar and the white cloth inside, the sink and the gas cooker, the unmade double bed, the armchair, the small table with the nebulizer, the window with the half-closed blinds and the crucifix, and the woman standing in the middle with her arms crossed and the man sitting in the armchair wrapped in the blanket, in the same places and poses. The two people must become drawn, deformed, grotesque characters, not photographs: strange caricatures rather than sick ones: exaggerated and distorted proportions, oversized and oddly shaped heads, eyes too big, too small or set too far apart, odd noses, long necks, big or long hands; their mouths closed, with the same tense, serious expressions as in the photo: no smiles, no grins, no visible teeth; unsettling and sinister, but healthy and well fed, with full cheeks and clean skin: never sick, wasted, dirty or dying, never cute or cartoonish. No text, no signature, no watermark.
STYLE: a 1970s European underground comic panel: bold black brush-ink outlines, expressive scratchy crosshatching, flat muted colors with no gradients (mustard, olive green, brick red, dirty beige), halftone dots in the shadows.

Remove the two people completely, with everything they hold. Reconstruct the empty room behind them naturally, in the same drawing style. Keep everything else exactly identical and in the same place: the cold wood stove with its door ajar and the white cloth inside, the sink and the gas cooker, the unmade double bed, the armchair, the small table with the nebulizer, the window with the half-closed blinds and the crucifix, the same lighting and the same camera. Do not draw any face anywhere.

Re-render only the two people as realistic photographs: real skin with pores, real hair, real fabric and real leather, photographic lighting. Keep exactly their grotesque, deformed features from this image: the same oversized, oddly shaped heads, the same strange eyes and noses, the same closed mouths and serious expressions, the same long necks and big or long hands, with healthy skin and full cheeks; the woman is in her fifties, with smooth, firm skin and only a few fine lines, the man in his seventies, big and strong (the hatching of the drawing is shading, not wrinkles), and the same proportions, silhouettes, poses, expressions, clothes and positions, pixel for pixel. Do not make them look more normal. Everything else in the image stays exactly identical.

Edit this comic drawing of an empty room. Keep exactly the same drawing style (bold black brush-ink outlines, flat muted colors with no gradients, light crosshatching only where there is shadow), the same composition and every object in exactly the same place and size. Clean only the walls and the ceiling: they become smooth, plain painted plaster in a warm off-white color, like a modest but cared-for home, with at most two or three faint damp stains. Remove all peeling and flaking paint, exposed patches, cracks, dirt streaks and texture marks that are not real objects. Do not add anything. No people, no faces, no text.

Re-render this drawing of an empty room as a realistic photograph, like an ordinary amateur snapshot, evenly exposed. The walls and the ceiling are smooth, plain painted plaster in a warm off-white color, like a modest but cared-for home, with at most two or three faint damp stains: do not copy the drawing's cracks, peeling or flaking paint, stains or hatching. Keep everything else exactly identical and in exactly the same place and size: the cold wood stove with its door ajar and the white cloth inside, the sink and the gas cooker, the unmade double bed, the armchair, the small table with the nebulizer, the window with the half-closed blinds and the crucifix, the lighting, the camera and the framing. Do not add any people, hands or objects, and no faces anywhere.

Change the two people in this image so that they look healthy but uncanny and wrong, like the 'alternates' of analog horror (The Mandela Catalogue), or like a familiar face that is different from how you remember it: something is off, even if at first you cannot say what. The woman standing in the middle: healthy, clean and well fed, with smooth, even, slightly waxy skin and only a few soft wrinkles for her sixty years; but her face is wrong: her eyes are a little too big and set a little too far apart, perfectly round, with very dark irises and a fixed, unblinking stare; her nose is small and too straight; her mouth is slightly too wide, pressed in a thin straight line; her face is a little too long and too symmetrical; her grey hair is neat and stiff, almost like a wig. The man in the armchair: healthy-looking for his seventy years, not thin, with clean, smooth, pinkish skin and a clean-shaven, round, bald head; but he is wrong: his head is slightly too big and too round; his pale eyes are a little too far apart and do not seem to blink; his ears sit a little too low; his upper lip is unnaturally long; his slightly open mouth shows too many small, even, white teeth; his hands are a little too large, with fingers slightly too long. The plastic tube of the nebulizer still hangs on his chest. Push these distortions further, so that the wrongness is obvious at first glance, while they still look like real people. Keep them as realistic photographs (real skin, hair and fabric), with the same clothes, poses, positions and lighting. They must not look sick, wasted, haggard, dirty or dying: healthy weight, clean skin, normal skin color, all their teeth, eyes with irises and pupils; not zombies, not monsters, not corpses. Do not change anything else in the image.
